planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring once frost risk has passed, giving the cinnamon-barked stems a full season to settle in before winter.

directions: This sport of Chilean myrtle keeps the species' cinnamon, peeling bark but adds a cream-gold margin to each small leaf, with new growth flushing pink before settling to green and gold. It holds its variegation best with some afternoon shade in hot climates and shelter from drying wind. Light, late-summer trimming keeps the habit dense without spoiling the following season's small white flowers.

planting.note: Set out container stock in fall so winter rains establish the roots before the dry California summer.

directions: This UC Davis selection of California's toyon swaps the species' familiar red winter berries for a glowing gold-orange fruit set against the same glossy, holly-like leaves. Growers also report it holding up better against the leaf-spot and fire-blight issues that sometimes trouble the straight species. It wants the same lean, fast-draining soil and minimal summer water as wild toyon and makes an excellent unclipped screen or wildlife hedge.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring once the soil has warmed; arching branches benefit from some room to spread.

directions: A graceful, fine-textured shrub from Yunnan and western Sichuan, its tiny ferny leaflets and arching stems are a favorite subject for bonsai as well as mixed borders. White hawthorn-like flowers in spring are followed by small white pome fruit that is edible and sometimes used for jam. Give it full sun and lean, well-drained soil; once established it shrugs off drought and needs little pruning beyond shaping.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once frost danger passes, into sharply drained soil.

directions: One of the showiest kunzeas in cultivation, this Western Australian shrub covers itself in dense crimson bottlebrush-like flower clusters from late autumn into spring. It wants sharp drainage and tolerates moderate frost once established, and responds well to a light trim after flowering to keep growth dense rather than leggy. Left unpruned it can be trained into a flowering screen or informal hedge.

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in spring; confine the roots, as this grass spreads aggressively by rhizome.

directions: This old cottage-garden standby brightens shade and damp ground with white-and-green striped blades on an otherwise ordinary running grass. It spreads fast by rhizome and is best given a buried barrier or grown in a large sunken container to keep it from overtaking a bed. Cutting it back hard in midsummer refreshes the foliage color after the first flush fades.

planting.note: Drill seed into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall for winter stratification, or as early as possible in spring.

directions: The plain species behind the widely planted 'Hycrest' hybrid, crested wheatgrass is the classic bunchgrass used across the semi-arid West for rangeland seeding and erosion control after fire or disturbance. It is extremely drought-hardy once established and tolerates heavy grazing better than most native grasses, which is why it remains a standard in reclamation seed mixes. Seedlings establish slowly, so keep competing weeds down the first year.

planting.note: Direct-seed shallowly into a firm seedbed as soon as the soil can be worked; stands take a full season to fill in.

directions: The plain species behind the named selection 'Bozoisky-Select,' Russian wildrye forms a dense, deep-rooted bunchgrass prized on the northern Great Plains for early, leafy spring forage and long persistence under dry conditions. Unlike many introduced grasses it stays mostly basal, growing in tight tussocks rather than spreading, which makes interseeding with it in old pasture relatively easy. It is slow to establish but outlasts most competing cool-season grasses once mature.

planting.note: Direct-sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.

directions: Grown throughout India as a rice substitute on land too dry or marginal for paddy, this fast-maturing millet is a close relative of the Japanese barnyard millet already grown for birdseed and wildlife plots. The grain cooks and threshes much like rice and is notably rich in iron and zinc compared with major cereals, while the leafy stalks double as livestock fodder. It thrives on minimal inputs and reaches harvest in about two to three months, making it useful as a quick catch crop.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Set out young plants in spring into sharply drained soil; avoid winter-wet sites.

directions: Unlike its low-growing relative kidney vetch, this is an upright Mediterranean coastal shrub grown mainly for its fine, silvery foliage and pale yellow spring flowers. It is a natural choice for seaside and gravel gardens, shrugging off salt spray, poor soil, and short hard frosts once its roots are established. Keep it on the dry side and in full sun, since soggy winter ground is its main weakness.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Drill seed into a prepared seedbed in early spring or late summer for pasture or hay.

directions: This is the plain tetraploid hybrid species behind named forage releases like 'Perun,' crossing meadow fescue with Italian ryegrass to combine fescue's drought and waterlogging tolerance with ryegrass's yield and palatability. It greens up early in spring with vigor close to annual ryegrass but persists like a perennial, making it useful in grass-legume mixtures for cutting or grazing. Forage researchers have favored it in grassland renewal trials as summers grow hotter and drier.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants after frost danger passes into well-drained, sandy soil.

directions: Named for bark that peels into tough, string-like strips, this compact shrub is valued in coastal and seaside plantings for its glossy foliage and tolerance of salt spray and poor soil. Small greenish-yellow flowers give way to bright red berries that glow against the dark leaves, though every part of the plant is toxic if eaten and should be sited away from children and grazing animals. It takes hard pruning well and is sometimes grown as a clipped seaside hedge.
sources: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery stock in spring; shears into a hedge easily once established.

directions: This purple-leaved selection of the pantropical hopseed bush is one of the most widely planted hedging and screening shrubs in the US Southwest and Australia, grown for its wine-red foliage that deepens with sun exposure. Papery, winged seed capsules follow the inconspicuous flowers and add a secondary season of color. It takes shearing hard and often, tolerates heat, wind, and poor soil, and is propagated from cuttings to keep the purple color true.

planting.note: Direct-sow outdoors after the last frost into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: A close but distinct cousin of Ursinia anethoides already in cultivation, this South African annual covers itself in daisy-like, two-toned blooms with bright rays and a dark central zone through summer and fall. It is easy from direct-sown seed, drought- and heat-tolerant once up, and best in lean, fast-draining soil where it won't flop or stretch. Deadheading extends the bloom season considerably.

planting.note: Transplant nursery seedlings during the warm, humid growing season.

directions: Distinct from the drier-climate Khaya senegalensis already grown, this rainforest mahogany is the primary source of commercial African mahogany timber and is planted as a fast-growing shade and avenue tree in frost-free, humid regions. It wants deep, moisture-retentive soil and consistent warmth, and young trees benefit from some shelter until their deep roots establish. Its flaking bark and dense, rounded crown make it a popular large shade tree well beyond its native West African forests.

subcategory: tropical flowering shade and timber tree

planting.note: Transplant seedlings during the warm season into deep, well-drained soil.

directions: The Philippine national tree and a different species from the drier-adapted West African Pterocarpus erinaceus already represented, narra is a fast-growing tropical hardwood planted throughout Southeast Asia as an avenue and shade tree for its wide, spreading canopy and brief but showy flushes of fragrant yellow flowers. Its buttressed trunk and durable, reddish timber have long made it valuable for furniture as well as landscaping. It tolerates poor, compacted urban soils far better than most large shade trees.
sources: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development (PCAARRD)

planting.note: Direct-sow scarified seed in fall so winter moisture breaks dormancy.

directions: Unlike the Mediterranean biennial Hedysarum coronarium already grown as a cover crop, this is a tough native perennial of the intermountain West, bearing racemes of magenta-pink, pea-like flowers that make it a favorite in pollinator and wildlife restoration seed mixes. It needs a cold, moist period to break seed dormancy and grows best in gravelly, fast-draining soil typical of its sagebrush-steppe habitat. Established plants are long-lived and extremely drought-tolerant.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide

planting.note: Pot divisions or tissue-cultured starts in spring once nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: This selected clone of the Australian pitcher plant produces notably larger pitchers than wild-collected plants, making it a favorite among carnivorous plant collectors. Grow it in a shallow tray of rainwater or distilled water over sphagnum moss, keeping the crown itself out of standing water. Provide bright, humid, cool-to-moderate conditions and let pitchers catch their own small insect prey rather than fertilizing. Propagate by division rather than seed to preserve the large-pitcher trait true to type.

planting.note: Install rhizome divisions in spring inside a buried root barrier to contain its running habit.

directions: This low, rapidly spreading dwarf bamboo makes a dense evergreen groundcover even in deep shade where few other plants thrive. Install divisions behind a buried root barrier or inside a sunken container, since its running rhizomes travel aggressively once established. Shear or mow the planting hard in late winter to refresh the foliage before new culms emerge. It tolerates both full sun and heavy shade, though leaf color stays richest with some protection from hot afternoon sun.

planting.note: Start seed indoors after cold stratification, then set plants out once frost danger has passed.

directions: This variegated sport of common pokeweed carries the same bold architecture as the wild species but with leaves heavily splashed in cream and pink along red stems. Start seed indoors after a cold stratification period, since germination is slower and less reliable than the plain green form. Site it in full sun to partial shade with room to reach several feet tall and wide, and cut off berry clusters before they ripen if children or pets have garden access, since every part of the plant remains toxic. Established clumps resprout reliably from the root each spring.

planting.note: Sow in a mineral cactus mix in spring and keep seedlings lightly shaded until they size up.

directions: This rare Mexican cactus forms a squat, deeply pleated gray-green body etched with fine wrinkles, eventually producing small pink flowers from its woolly crown. Sow seed in a mineral, fast-draining mix and keep seedlings lightly shaded, since this species grows markedly slower than most columnar cacti. Water sparingly on a strict dry-between cycle and withhold water almost entirely during winter dormancy. Many growers graft young seedlings onto vigorous understock to speed up early development.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow on the surface of sandy mineral grit in spring and mist lightly until germination occurs.

directions: This window-leaved succulent forms clumps of club-shaped, translucent-tipped leaves that sit nearly flush with the soil surface, much as it does in its native habitat. Sow seed on the surface of sandy, mineral grit and mist lightly until germination, then switch to infrequent bottom watering as the clump matures. Give it the brightest light available and let the mix dry completely between waterings to avoid rot. Established clusters send up daisy-like orange flowers that open fully only in direct sun.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Transplant container-grown palms into full sun in late spring once soil has fully warmed.

directions: Known as the Cuban wax palm, this stately fan palm develops a thick, smooth trunk and a dense, rounded crown of silvery-green fronds as it matures. Transplant container-grown palms into full sun once soil has warmed in late spring, giving them ample room since mature specimens eventually reach impressive height and girth. It tolerates both drought and brief cold once established, which has made it a popular specimen palm in warm, frost-free landscapes. Growth is slow from seed, so most gardeners buy larger nursery specimens rather than starting from scratch.

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery stock in spring into sharply draining soil, since own-root plants are prone to root disease.

directions: Qualup bell produces pendant, bell-shaped flower heads wrapped in cream bracts streaked with red, among the showiest blooms in its genus. Because own-root plants are highly prone to root disease, most nursery stock is grafted onto a more vigorous Pimelea understock for reliability. Plant grafted specimens in spring into very sharply draining soil in full sun, avoiding the humid, muggy conditions this species cannot tolerate. Once established it is fairly drought tolerant but benefits from excellent air movement around its base.

planting.note: Pot rooted cuttings in gritty cactus mix in spring and repot as the clustering stems fill their container.

directions: This popular monstrose form grows as a cluster of unevenly branching, four-angled green stems that resemble miniature turrets, giving the cultivar its common name. Pot rooted cuttings in a gritty, fast-draining cactus mix and set them in bright, direct light for the most compact growth. Water only once the soil has dried completely and withhold water almost entirely through winter. Mature indoor specimens rarely flower, but outdoor plants in warm climates can eventually produce large, fragrant night-blooming flowers.

planting.note: Mount bare-root divisions on bark or pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix in spring.

directions: Bear's paw fern takes its name from the thick, fuzzy brown rhizomes that creep across the surface of its growing medium or host tree, resembling furry paws. Mount bare-root divisions on a slab of bark or pot them in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix, leaving part of the rhizome exposed to light and air. Grow it in bright, indirect light with high humidity and consistent moisture, since the fronds scorch quickly in direct sun. It is reliably hardy only in frost-free climates and is otherwise grown as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen.

planting.note: Transplant young trees into a sheltered site in spring, protecting them from harsh winter wind while they establish.

directions: Roble beech is a fast-growing South American relative of true beech, prized in large gardens for handsome foliage that turns gold, orange, and crimson in autumn. Transplant container-grown trees into a sheltered site protected from harsh winter wind, since young plants can be badly damaged by exposure before they establish. It prefers moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and performs best where summers stay cool. It remains a specialist tree in cultivation but is increasingly offered by arboretum-affiliated and specialist tree nurseries.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown plugs or bare-root culms into loose sand in spring and water just enough to establish roots.

directions: European beachgrass is a tough, rhizomatous grass long used to stabilize shifting coastal dunes, sending up stiff, gray-green blades from deeply running roots. Plant nursery-grown plugs or bare-root culms into loose sand in spring, watering just enough to establish roots before leaving the planting to fend for itself. It thrives on wind-blown sand burial, pushing new shoots upward as dunes build around it, but spreads aggressively and can crowd out native dune vegetation. Because of its invasive tendencies outside its native range, check local regulations before planting it intentionally.
sources: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board

planting.note: Float plantlets directly on the water surface once pond or tank water has warmed in spring.

directions: Amazon frogbit floats freely on still or slow-moving water, forming rosettes of glossy, rounded leaves with long trailing roots that shade and filter the water column. Simply float plantlets on the surface of a pond or aquarium in bright, indirect to full sun and let it multiply by producing offsets. It grows quickly in nutrient-rich water, so thin colonies regularly to keep it from shading out submerged plants. Protect it from hard freezes, since it is damaged below about 50°F and will not survive outdoor winters in cold climates.

planting.note: Let stem cuttings callus for several days before potting into a very open, mineral succulent mix in spring.

directions: This South African stapeliad produces unusually large, trumpet-shaped flowers covered in fine hairs and marked with maroon bands, carried on low clumps of slender, toothed stems. Propagate from stem cuttings allowed to callus for several days before potting into a very open, mineral succulent mix. Keep it in bright light with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun, watering sparingly and letting the mix dry out between waterings. Like its stapeliad relatives, the flowers give off a faint carrion scent that attracts fly pollinators.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Direct sow or divide clumps after soil has warmed in spring.

directions: Smilo Grass forms airy, fountain-like clumps of fine foliage topped by loose, open seedheads that catch the light and sway in the slightest breeze. It self-sows readily in Mediterranean-type climates, so many gardeners treat it as a reseeding annual or divide and relocate seedlings each year. Plant it in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, since rich conditions can make it floppy. Established clumps are quite drought tolerant and need little supplemental water once rooted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun and sharply drained soil; extremely slow growing.

directions: Blue Needle Palm is an extremely slow-growing, cold-hardy palm from the dry grasslands of Argentina and Uruguay, prized for its stiff, steely blue-gray fan leaves tipped with sharp spines. It thrives in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, tolerating both drought and surprisingly cold winters once established. Because it may take decades to form a visible trunk, it is usually grown as a long-term specimen rather than a quick landscape fix. Protect young plants from prolonged wet, cold conditions, which are more damaging than cold alone.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil with shelter from wind and hot afternoon sun.

directions: This Chilean woodland shrub produces hundreds of waxy, crimson, lantern-shaped flowers dangling from thin stalks in late spring and early summer, a striking contrast against glossy dark evergreen foliage. It performs best in the dappled light of a woodland garden or on the shaded side of a wall, since direct hot sun and dry soil quickly scorch the leaves. Give it acidic, consistently moist, well-drained soil amended with leaf mold, and mulch the roots to keep them cool through summer. It is slow to establish but eventually forms a dense, upright, multi-stemmed specimen prized in Pacific Northwest and coastal climates.

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained soil with shelter from cold wind; tolerates woodland-edge part shade better than most lacebarks.

directions: A hardy New Zealand hybrid lacebark valued for glossy evergreen foliage and a late-summer flush of small white flowers that draw pollinators when little else is blooming. It accepts part shade at the edge of larger trees far more readily than open-grown lacebark species, making it useful for softening shaded boundaries or courtyards. Growth is upright and fairly fast once established, and light pruning after flowering keeps the habit tidy. Give it shelter from harsh winter wind in its early years, after which it handles occasional frost without serious dieback.

planting.note: Divide or plant offsets in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil; established clumps resent disturbance.

directions: This Chatham Island tussock forms a bold fountain of arching, metallic silver-grey strap leaves that reads as sculpture in a shaded border, and it is one of the few truly silver-foliaged perennials that performs in low light rather than scorching there. Clumps build slowly from a woody crown and are best left undivided for several years to reach full architectural size. It appreciates shelter from drying wind, which can fray the leaf tips, and benefits from a thick mulch in colder parts of its range. Established plants shrug off coastal salt spray and light frost equally well.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant divisions in spring into well-drained soil; tolerates light shade under high canopy.

directions: This evergreen New Zealand iris relative forms tight fans of narrow, orange-gold-flushed leaves that intensify in cooler weather, giving winter color to shaded beds where flowering plants have gone dormant. Small white starry flowers appear on wiry stems in late spring, followed by orange seed capsules that add further interest. It spreads gently by rhizome and self-seeding without becoming aggressive, and clumps can be lifted and divided every few years to rejuvenate the planting. Good drainage prevents the crown from rotting over winter, especially in heavier shaded soils.

planting.note: Plant after frost danger has passed against a trellis or shaded fence in well-drained soil.

directions: A white-flowered form of the Australian native vine usually seen in violet-purple, carrying the same dense late-winter sprays of small pea flowers against twining, leathery evergreen foliage. It climbs readily on a trellis or low fence and tolerates the filtered light under open-canopy trees, flowering less heavily in deep shade but still performing better there than many flowering vines. Once established it is drought tolerant and needs only an occasional light prune after bloom to control size and encourage denser flowering wood. Where marginally hardy, grow it against a sheltered shaded wall that buffers winter cold.
